newsitem.title: CHINA: China launches fresh crackdown on futures markets.
newsitem.headline: China launches fresh crackdown on futures markets.

text.p: China is launching a fresh crackdown on its fledging futures markets, and the move could lead to the closure of most of the 15 existing exchanges, analysts said on Thursday.
In the past week, the authorities have issued two documents emphasising curbs rather than expansion as the keynote of the futures markets, at least for the time being.

The principal aim is "to take effective measures to clean up and rectify the futures market, strengthen supervision and curb excessive speculation," a document issued by the State Council, the cabinet, said on Wednesday.

In a separate notice published last Saturday, the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) said there were serious problems including continued foreign exchange margin trading and overseas futures trading, despite repeated bans.
"This is the most severe crackdown since the one in 1993," said a commodity investment analyst with a major Chinese futures brokerage.
"Trading in more than half of the existing exchanges has been very light and they have lost their function as a futures market for hedging and pricing," a commodity futures analyst said.

"With only small contracts available, some futures markets have become hotbeds of irregularities," said another analyst. "In addition, compared with some advanced countries, China has too many futures markets and should be able to close some."
Analysts said exchanges under threat include those in Suzhou, Chengdu and Chongqing.
The authorities might initially order larger markets such as Shanghai to take over smaller markets instead of ordering their outright closure in order to limit the negative impact, they said.
The new measures reflect Beijing's increasing anger at being unable to control excessive speculation on the commodity futures markets effectively, they said.
Violations of the trading rules are rampant and large amounts of state assets have been gambled and lost on the markets, analysts added.

"The central government is very angry that some major firms including some futures brokerages defy repeated bans and continue to do forbidden business such as foreign exchange margin trading," said a metal futures trader.
"Most of the firms are run by the state and some lose huge amounts of money not only on domestic futures markets but also outside the country," he added.
Rumours about the fresh crackdown began to circulate in the markets as early as mid-September, pushing down most futures prices.
Dozens of futures exchanges opened across China in the early 1990s, but Beijing has since ordered most of them to close, allowing only 15 to continue to run on a trial basis.
In Wednesday's document, the State Council said that instead of the futures markets, it encouraged "the active and steady development of the stock market."
Beijing has allowed a record number of firms to be listed on both the Shanghai and Shenzhen bourses this year.

Echoing the new move, the official Business News on Sunday urged Chinese investors to stay out of the futures markets and to concentrate on stocks, leaving futures to major companies wishing to hedge risk.
